title: Gold triple-finger ring

altText: A gold ring made to be worn across three fingers at once, set with glass. It is an unusual piece of Roman jewelry from the eastern part of the Empire.

context: A gold ring made to fit across three fingers, with glass set into it, dated to the 3rd to 4th century CE and labeled Roman, Syrian. Gold and glass were both prized jewelry materials in the late Roman world.

descriptions.k: This ring is not for one finger. It fits across three fingers! It is made of gold and glass. People in the Roman world wore it. Can you imagine wearing it? What would you do with your hand?
descriptions.g12: This gold ring was made to fit on three fingers at the same time. It has pieces of glass set in it that shine. Someone made it in the Roman world, in a region called Syria, about 1,700 years ago. Look for where the glass sits in the gold. Why would someone want a ring this big?
descriptions.g35: Most rings fit one finger, but this gold ring was made to wear across three. It combines gold with glass pieces that were set into it, and it was made in the Roman world in the Syrian region around the 3rd or 4th century CE. Look at how the gold holds each piece of glass. How would wearing it change the way you use your hand?
descriptions.g68: This triple-finger ring from the late Roman period, labeled Roman, Syrian in the Met's record, is made of gold and glass. Gold and colorful stones or glass were prized for jewelry, and a ring spanning three fingers makes a bold statement. Look at how the goldsmith organizes the settings across the width of the ring. What does a large piece of jewelry like this suggest about its wearer's wealth, taste, and priorities?
descriptions.g910: A triple-finger ring turns the hand into a display, extending the usual single focus of a ring across three fingers. The combination of gold and glass settings shows the late Roman interest in color and bright effects. Because the ring would restrict how fingers move, it may have been worn for show rather than daily work, but the record does not state its use. Consider how scale, material, and the body's constraints shape the design, and what the ring suggests about display and status.
descriptions.g1112: This ring belongs to the late Roman world's taste for polychrome jewelry, where gold is paired with colorful inserts, here glass. Its triple-finger form raises questions of function and display, since wearing it would limit the hand's movement, and the record does not tell us who wore it or in what setting. The classification as Roman, Syrian points to regional workshops within the wider Empire. Consider how jewelry can shape posture and gesture, and how we weigh the evidence of an unusual shape against an unknown owner.

teacherNote.context: A gold and glass ring made to fit three fingers, dated to the 3rd to 4th century CE and labeled Roman, Syrian in the Met's record. It shows how jewelry styles varied across the Roman world.
directions: Have students trace their hand and design a ring that spans three fingers, noting how it would limit movement.
Locate Syria and Rome on a map and discuss how the Roman Empire included many regions with their own styles.
Compare gold and glass: what does each material do with light, and why combine them?
